nameStory: This mountain wildflower gets its "rattlesnake root" name from the belief that its milky sap could cure snakebites, though this folk remedy has no scientific basis. The "alpine" part refers to its love of high, cold places in the mountains. It's also called Boott's rattlesnake root after John Wright Boott, the Boston botanist who first collected it in New Hampshire's White Mountains back in 1829.
description: Alpine rattlesnake root is a rare mountain wildflower that belongs to the sunflower family, though you'd never guess it from its small, drooping bell-shaped flowers. This perennial plant grows 1-3 feet tall with a single, sturdy stem and produces clusters of pale yellow to cream-colored flowers that hang downward like tiny lanterns. It's found only in the highest, coldest parts of New England's mountains, making it a special treat for dedicated hikers. Like other rattlesnake roots, it has a milky sap that oozes from broken stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, pale yellow to cream bell-shaped flowers that droop downward in loose clusters, completely unlike the typical daisy-like flowers you'd expect from the sunflower family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Triangular to heart-shaped leaves that feel smooth to the touch and are arranged alternately up the stem, often with slightly toothed edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched stem rising 1-3 feet from the ground, giving the plant a simple, elegant appearance in alpine settings

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Milky white sap that oozes out when you break the stem - this latex-like fluid is characteristic of all rattlesnake roots

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white seed heads that form after flowering, with feathery plumes that catch mountain breezes for dispersal

habitat: You'll only find this rare plant in the highest elevations of New England's mountains, typically above 3,000 feet in alpine zones and subalpine areas. It grows in rocky crevices, talus slopes, and thin soils among mountain peaks, particularly in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and similar high-elevation sites in Vermont and Maine. Look for it in areas where harsh winds and short growing seasons keep other plants at bay.

seasonality.spring: Young leaves begin emerging from rocky crevices as snow melts in late spring, but flowering won't begin for several weeks.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from July through August with its distinctive drooping pale flowers, making this the best time for identification in its remote mountain habitat.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to fluffy white seed heads that persist into early fall before dispersing on mountain winds.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no trace above the snow-covered alpine landscape.

funFact: This is one of New England's rarest wildflowers, with only 51 recorded observations ever documented - you're more likely to spot a black bear on the mountain than find this elusive alpine treasure!
confusionNotes: The drooping, bell-shaped flowers make this unlikely to be confused with most other mountain plants, but it could be mistaken for other rattlesnake roots at lower elevations. Remember: if you're not above treeline or in serious alpine terrain, you're probably looking at a different rattlesnake root species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the scary name "rattlesnake root," these plants have nothing to do with actual rattlesnakes and the folk remedy use is purely historical. The milky sap is harmless but can be mildly irritating to sensitive skin.
compareHints: Alpine rattlesnake root is much smaller and more delicate than its lowland cousins like tall rattlesnake root, and its flowers are distinctly pale yellow rather than purple or white. Unlike white rattlesnake root which can grow quite tall in rich forest soils, alpine rattlesnake root stays compact to survive harsh mountain conditions. The key difference is habitat - if you're not huffing and puffing at high elevation, you're looking at a different species!

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its rattlesnake root relatives, three-leaved rattlesnake root is distinguished by its trifoliate leaves - most others have simple, undivided leaves.
Tall rattlesnake root lives up to its name by being the tallest of the New England rattlesnake roots, often reaching 6 feet compared to the 2-3 foot height of white rattlesnake root.
Among New England's rattlesnake roots, white rattlesnake root has the smallest flower heads and the most variable leaf shapes.

Lion's foot rattlesnake root stands out from its rattlesnake root relatives by having the most dramatically lobed leaves - they're much more deeply cut than white rattlesnake root's triangular leaves or tall rattlesnake root's broader, less-divided foliage.
Purple rattlesnake root stands apart from its relatives by preferring wet habitats while most other rattlesnake roots grow in dry woods or clearings.
